tea:anapanasati-sutta:mn118:26.title: Ānāpānasati Sutta
tea:anapanasati-sutta:mn118:26.original: Yasmiṁ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu ‘cittapaṭisaṁvedī assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘cittapaṭisaṁvedī passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘abhippamodayaṁ cittaṁ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘abhippamodayaṁ cittaṁ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘samādahaṁ cittaṁ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘samādahaṁ cittaṁ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; ‘vimocayaṁ cittaṁ assasissāmī’ti sikkhati, ‘vimocayaṁ cittaṁ passasissāmī’ti sikkhati; citte cittānupassī, bhikkhave, tasmiṁ samaye bhikkhu viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ. Nāhaṁ, bhikkhave, muṭṭhassatissa asampajānassa ānāpānassatiṁ vadāmi. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, citte cittānupassī tasmiṁ samaye bhikkhu viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ.
tea:anapanasati-sutta:mn118:26.paraphrase: At the time when a monk trains in experiencing the mind, gladdening the mind, concentrating the mind and liberating the mind (the third tetrad), at that time he abides contemplating mind in mind, ardent (ātāpī), clearly comprehending (sampajāna) and mindful (satimā), having put away covetousness and displeasure for the world. The Buddha says: 'I do not speak of mindfulness of breathing for one of muddled mindfulness (muṭṭhassati) and without clear comprehension (asampajāna); therefore at that time the monk abides contemplating mind in mind'.

tea:bhagavad-gita:16.4.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:16.4.original: dambho darpo'bhimānaśca krodhaḥ pāruṣyameva ca|ajñānaṃ cābhijātasya pārtha sampadamāsurīm
tea:bhagavad-gita:16.4.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: hypocrisy (dambha), arrogance (darpa), conceit (abhimāna), anger (krodha), harshness (pāruṣya) and ignorance (ajñāna) belong, Pārtha, to one born to the demonic endowment (āsurī sampad).

tea:bhagavad-gita:16.5.title: Bhagavad Gītā
tea:bhagavad-gita:16.5.original: daivī sampadvimokṣāya nibandhāyāsurī matā|mā śucaḥ sampadaṃ daivīmabhijāto'si pāṇḍava
tea:bhagavad-gita:16.5.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: the divine endowment is held to lead to release (vimokṣa), the demonic to bondage (nibandha). Do not grieve (mā śucaḥ), Pāṇḍava: you are born to the divine endowment.

tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:1.4.10.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:1.4.10.original: brahma vā idam agra āsīt tad ātmānam evāvet ahaṃ brahmāsmīti tasmāt tat sarvam abhavat
tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:1.4.10.paraphrase: In the beginning this was brahman; it knew only itself: 'I am brahman' (ahaṃ brahmāsmi); therefore it became all. Whoever among the gods, the seers and humans awoke to it became that. Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva declared 'I was Manu and the sun'. Even now whoever knows 'I am brahman' becomes this all; even the gods cannot prevent it, for he becomes their self. But whoever venerates another deity, thinking 'he is one, I am another', does not know; he is like a domestic animal for the gods.

tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:3.4.1-2.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
tea:brhadaranyaka-upanisad:3.4.1-2.paraphrase: Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa: 'explain to me the brahman that is immediate and direct, the self within all.' 'It is your self that is within all. You cannot see the seer of seeing, hear the hearer of hearing, think the thinker of thinking, understand the understander of understanding. This is your self within all; everything other than it is sorrowful (ārta).'

tea:chandogya-upanisad:6.8.7.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
tea:chandogya-upanisad:6.8.7.original: sa ya eṣo 'ṇimaitadātmyam idaṃ sarvaṃ tat satyaṃ sa ātmā tat tvam asi śvetaketo iti
tea:chandogya-upanisad:6.8.7.paraphrase: That which is the finest essence — this whole world has it as its self; that is the real; that is the self; that you are (tat tvam asi), Śvetaketu. 'Teach me further, sir.' 'So be it, dear one.' The refrain recurs at the close of each of the following illustrations (6.9.4 to 6.16.3; nine times in all).

tea:chandogya-upanisad:8.12.1-2.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
tea:chandogya-upanisad:8.12.1-2.paraphrase: This body is mortal, held by death; it is the base of the immortal, bodiless self. One who has a body is held by pleasure and pain; for one who has a body there is no end to pleasure and pain; but pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless. Wind, clouds, lightning and thunder are bodiless.

tea:dhammapada:279.title: Dhammapada
tea:dhammapada:279.original: “Sabbe dhammā anattā”ti, yadā paññāya passati; Atha nibbindati dukkhe, esa maggo visuddhiyā.
tea:dhammapada:279.paraphrase: 'All dhammas are not-self (anattā)': when one sees this with wisdom, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.

tea:mandukya-upanisad:2.title: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
tea:mandukya-upanisad:2.original: sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt
tea:mandukya-upanisad:2.paraphrase: For all this is brahman; this self (ātman) is brahman; and this same self has four quarters (catuṣpād).

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:3.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:3.original: Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ; citte cittānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ; dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṁ. Uddeso niṭṭhito.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:3.paraphrase: The Buddha asks which four and answers. Here a monk abides contemplating the body in the body (kāye kāyānupassī), feelings in feelings (vedanāsu vedanānupassī), mind in mind (citte cittānupassī), and dhammas in dhammas (dhammesu dhammānupassī): in each case ardent (ātāpī), clearly comprehending (sampajāna) and mindful (satimā), having put away covetousness and displeasure (abhijjhādomanassa) with regard to the world. The statement of the theme (uddesa) ends.

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:40.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:40.original: 4.3. Dhammānupassanāāyatanapabba Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuñca pajānāti, rūpe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Sotañca pajānāti, sadde ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Ghānañca pajānāti, gandhe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Jivhañca pajānāti, rase ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Kāyañca pajānāti, phoṭṭhabbe ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti. Manañca pajānāti, dhamme ca pajānāti, yañca tadubhayaṁ paṭicca uppajjati saṁyojanaṁ tañca pajānāti, yathā ca anuppannassa saṁyojanassa uppādo hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca uppannassa saṁyojanassa pahānaṁ hoti tañca pajānāti, yathā ca pahīnassa saṁyojanassa āyatiṁ anuppādo hoti tañca pajānāti.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:40.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, third section: the six internal and external sense bases (āyatana). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas with regard to them. Here a monk knows the eye and knows forms, and he knows the fetter (saṁyojana) that arises dependent on both; he knows how an unarisen fetter comes to arise, how an arisen fetter is abandoned, and how an abandoned fetter will not arise again in the future. He does the same for the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and dhammas.

tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:41.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:41.original: Iti ajjhattaṁ vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, bahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati, ajjhattabahiddhā vā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati; samudayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati, samudayavayadhammānupassī vā dhammesu viharati. ‘Atthi dhammā’ti vā panassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti. Yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya paṭissatimattāya anissito ca viharati na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesu. Āyatanapabbaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ.
tea:satipatthana-sutta:mn10:41.paraphrase: The refrain. Thus he abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas internally, or externally, or both internally and externally; he abides contemplating the nature of arising (samudayadhamma) in the dhammas, or the nature of passing away (vayadhamma), or the nature of both arising and passing away. Or else mindfulness that 'there is dhammas' is established in him just to the extent of knowledge and recollection (ñāṇamatta, paṭissatimatta); he abides independent (anissita) and clings to nothing in the world (na ca kiñci loke upādiyati). Thus too the monk abides contemplating dhammas in dhammas. The section on the sense bases ends, with the closing line: thus the monk abides contemplating dhammas with regard to the six internal and external sense bases.

tea:tattvartha-sutra:10.9.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:10.9.paraphrase: [The liberated] are to be set out (sādhya) by: region (kṣetra), time (kāla), destiny (gati), mark (liṅga), tīrtha, conduct (cāritra), enlightenment as a pratyekabuddha or by another (pratyekabuddha-bodhita), knowledge (jñāna), extent of occupied space (avagāhanā), interval (antara), number (saṅkhyā) and relative fewness or greatness (alpa-bahutva).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:2.1.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:2.1.original: aupaśamikakṣāyikau bhāvau miśraśca jīvasya svatattvamaudayikapāriṇāmikau ca
tea:tattvartha-sutra:2.1.paraphrase: The states (bhāva) of the soul (jīva) are the subsidential (aupaśamika), the destructional (kṣāyika) and the mixed (miśra); and the rising (audayika) and the inherent (pāriṇāmika). These are the soul's own nature (svatattva).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:2.7.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:2.7.paraphrase: And (ca) the inherent states (pāriṇāmika) are being a soul (jīvatva), capability of liberation (bhavyatva) and incapability of it (abhavyatva).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:7.12.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:7.12.paraphrase: Or (vā) the nature (svabhāva) of the world (jagat) and of the body (kāya) is to be reflected on, for the sake of dread of saṃsāra (saṃvega) and detachment (vairāgya).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.11.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.11.paraphrase: Body-making karma (nāma) includes: destiny (gati), class (jāti), body (śarīra), limbs (aṅga, upāṅga), formation (nirmāṇa), binding (bandhana), aggregation (saṅghāta), shape (saṃsthāna), joints (saṃhanana), touch, taste, smell and colour, the migratory form (ānupūrvya), the neither-heavy-nor-light (agurulaghu), self-injuring (upaghāta), other-injuring (paraghāta), heat (ātapa), light (udyota), breath (ucchvāsa) and gait (vihāyogati); and, in pairs with their opposites, individual body (pratyeka-śarīra) and mobility (trasa), attractiveness (subhaga), sweet voice (susvara), auspiciousness (śubha), subtlety (sūkṣma), completion (paryāpti), stability (sthira), impressiveness (ādeya), fame (yaśas-kīrti); and the Tīrthaṅkara state (tīrthakaratva).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.2.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.2.original: sakaṣāyatvājjīvaḥ karmaṇo yogyān pudgalānādatte sa baṃdhaḥ
tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.2.paraphrase: Because it has passions (sakaṣāyatvāt), the soul (jīva) takes in the material particles (pudgala) that are fit to be karma: that is bondage (bandha).

tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.9.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:8.9.paraphrase: Deluding karma (mohanīya) is named as view-deluding (darśana-mohanīya), conduct-deluding (cāritra-mohanīya), non-passion-felt (akaṣāya-vedanīya) and passion-felt (kaṣāya-vedanīya), with three, two, nine and sixteen kinds respectively. View-deluding: right view (samyaktva), wrong view (mithyātva) and both (tad-ubhaya). Conduct-deluding: non-passion and passion (akaṣāya, kaṣāya). Non-passions: laughter, liking, disliking, grief, fear, disgust, and the female, male and neuter sex-drive (vedas). The passions are the four, anger (krodha), pride (māna), deceit (māyā) and greed (lobha), each with four varieties (vikalpa) named anantānubandhī ("bound to the endless"), apratyākhyāna ("non-renunciation"), pratyākhyāna ("renunciation") and saṃjvalana ("flaring together"); these glosses give only the literal sense of the names.

tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.7.title: Tattvārthasūtra
tea:tattvartha-sutra:9.7.paraphrase: The anuprekṣās (repeated contemplations) are anucintana of: impermanence (anitya), no refuge (aśaraṇa), the round of births (saṃsāra), aloneness (ekatva), otherness (anyatva), impurity (aśuci), inflow (āsrava), stopping (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), the universe (loka), the rarity of enlightenment (bodhi-durlabha), and the well-taught nature of dharma (dharma-svākhyātatva).

tea:visuddhimagga:14.p469.paraphrase: Wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is that by which one sees wrongly, or which sees wrongly, or mere wrong seeing: its mark is unwise insistence; its function is clinging; its manifestation is wrong adherence; its proximate cause is the wish not to see the noble ones and the like; it is to be regarded as the most blameworthy. Restlessness (uddhacca) is agitated state: its mark is non-calming; its function is unsteadiness, like water stirred by wind; its manifestation is bewilderment, like a flag fluttering in the wind or like ashes thrown up by a blow on a stone; its proximate cause is unwise attention to the non-calming of the mind; it is to be regarded as distraction of consciousness. The other factors are as stated for the unwholesome. The second unwholesome consciousness is like the first, but prompted and with sloth-torpor indeterminate. Sloth (thīna) is the sinking, torpor (middha) the drowsing: sloth has as its mark lack of energy and as function dispelling energy, as manifestation sinking; torpor has as mark unworkableness, as function smothering, as manifestation drooping or drowsy sleep; for both the proximate cause is unwise attention to discontent, lazy stretching and the like. Conceit (māna), indeterminate in the third and fourth, has as mark haughtiness, as function self-promotion, as manifestation vain-glory, as proximate cause greed dissociated from view; it is to be regarded as madness. The fifth to eighth are given in the same manner without wrong view or with joy left out.

appavisayāni itarāni catucittasampayogā| yebhuyyena ca  
ālayarāmattā pajāya pākaṭaṃ kāmūpādānaṃ, na itarāni|  
kāmūpādānaṃ vā kāmānaṃ samadhigamatthaṃ kotū-  
halamangalādi-bahulo hoti; sassatan ti tad-anantaraṃ diṭṭhū-  
pādānaṃ| taṃ pabhijjamānaṃ sīlabbata-attavādūpādā-  
navasena duvidhaṃ hoti| tasmiṃ dvaye gokiriyaṃ kuk-  
kurakiriyaṃ vā disvā pi veditabbato: oḷārikan ti sīlabbatū-  
pādānaṃ paṭhamaṃ desitaṃ; sukhumattā ante attavādū-  
pādānan ti ayam etesaṃ desanākkamo|
tea:visuddhimagga:17.p570.paraphrase: Continuation. Clinging to rites and observances is quoted as the view "purity by virtue, by observance, by virtue-and-observance"; clinging to a doctrine of self is the twenty-fold view of a personal existence (sakkāyadiṭṭhi): "here the uninstructed ordinary person regards form as self" and so on. This is the summary of the states. On order: the order is threefold: of arising, of abandoning and of teaching. Since in a beginningless round there is no first arising of the defilements, the order of arising is not strictly stated, but in a manner of speaking, in one existence the clinging to a doctrine of self comes first, then adherence to eternalism or annihilationism: one who grasps "the self is eternal" takes up rites and observances for the purity of the self; one who grasps "it is annihilated", indifferent to another world, takes up sense pleasures; then views, rites and sense pleasures. In the order of abandoning, clinging to views and the rest are abandoned first, being to be cut by the stream-entry path, and clinging to sensual pleasures last, being to be cut by the arahat path. In the order of teaching, sense pleasures are taught first for their wide scope and evidence; then views; and of these two, rites and observances (coarse, seen in the behaviour of cows and dogs) before the doctrine of self (subtle).

tea:visuddhimagga:20.p638.title: Visuddhimagga
tea:visuddhimagga:20.p638.original:
ñāṇaṃ |||pe||| nikantiṃ: n'; etaṃ mama, n'; eso 'ham  
asmi, na me so attā ti samanupassati| evaṃ samanupassanto  
obhāsādisu na kampati na vedhati| ten'; āhu porāṇā:-  
          imāni dasa ṭhānāni paññā yassa parīcitā,  
          dhammuddhaccakusalo hoti na ca vikkhepam gacchatī ti|  
     so evaṃ vikkhepaṃ agacchanto taṃ samatiṃsavidhaṃ  
upakkilesajaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā: obhāsādayo dhammā na maggo,  
upakkilesavimuttaṃ pana vīthipaṭipannaṃ vipassanāñāṇam  
maggo ti maggañ ca amaggañ ca vavatthapeti| tass'; evaṃ  
ayaṃ maggo, ayaṃ na maggo ti maggañ ca amaggañ ca  
ñatvā ṭhitaṃ ñāṇaṃ maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhī ti  
veditabbaṃ|  
                     [tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ]  
     ettāvatā ca pana tena tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ  
kataṃ hoti| kathaṃ? diṭṭhivisuddhiyaṃ tāva nāma-  
rūpassa vavatthāpanena, dukkhasaccassa vavatthānaṃ  
kataṃ; kankhāvitaraṇavisuddhiyaṃ paccayapariggahaṇena  
samudayasaccassa vavatthānaṃ, imissa maggāmaggañā-  
ṇadassanavisuddhiyaṃ sammāmaggassa avadhāraṇena magga-  
saccassa vavatthānaṃ katan ti| evaṃ lokiyen'; eva tāva  
ñāṇena tiṇṇaṃ saccānaṃ vavatthānaṃ kataṃ hoti|  
iti sādhujanapāmojjatthāya kate visuddhi-magge paññā-  
bhāvanādhikāre maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhiniddeso  
nāma vīsatimo paricchedo|
tea:visuddhimagga:20.p638.paraphrase: Concluding the imperfections: he regards illumination, knowledge and the rest as "this is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self", and so regarding does not waver or tremble at them. The ancients say: one whose understanding is practised in these ten spots is skilled in restlessness about the Dhamma and is not distracted. So not distracted, he unpicks the thirty-fold tangle of imperfections and defines the path and the not-path: illumination and the rest are not the path; the insight-knowledge that has entered the true course, free of imperfections, is the path. The knowledge that stands, knowing the path and the not-path, is the purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path. At this point he has defined the three truths: by defining mind-and-matter in the purification of view he has defined suffering; by discerning conditions in the purification by overcoming doubt, the origin; by determining the right path here, the path. The chapter ends with the colophon, the twentieth chapter.

tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.title: Visuddhimagga
tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.original:
gatā1 kāmarāgasaṃyojanā paṭighasaṃyojanā aṇusahagatā kā-  
marāgānusayā paṭighānusayā vuṭṭhāti |||pe||| arahatta-  
maggakkhaṇe dassan'; aṭṭhena sammādiṭṭhi | | | avikkhepan'  
aṭṭhena sammāsamādhi, rūparāgā arūparāgā mānā | | | ud-  
dhaccā | | | avijjāya mānānusayā bhavarāgānusayā avijjānu-  
sayā vuṭṭhāti, tad-anuvattakakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭ-  
ṭhāti, bahiddhā ca sabbanimittehi vuṭṭhāti, tena vuccati: dubhato  
vuṭṭhānavivaṭṭane paññā magge ñāṇan ti2|  
     lokiyānañ ca aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ bhāvanākāle sam-  
athabalaṃ adhikaṃ hoti; aniccānupassanādīnaṃ bhāvanā-  
kāle vipassanābalaṃ| ariyamaggakhaṇe pana yuganandhā  
te dhammā pavattanti aññamaññaṃ anativattan'; aṭṭhena;  
tasmā imesu catusu pi ñāṇesu ubhayabalasamāyogo hoti|  
yath'; āha:- uddhaccasahagatakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭ-  
ṭhahato cittassa ekaggatā avikkhepo samādhi nirodhagocaro|  
avijjāsahagatakilesehi ca khandhehi ca vuṭṭhahato anupassan'  
aṭṭhena vipassanā nirodhagocarā| iti vuṭṭhān'; aṭṭhena samatha-  
vipassanā ekarasā honti, ayuganandhā honti, aññamaññaṃ  
nātivattantī ti, tena vuccati vuṭṭhān'; aṭṭhena samathavipassanaṃ  
yuganandhaṃ bhāvetī ti3|  
     evam ettha vuṭṭhānabalasamāyogo veditabbo|  
                              [c| pahānaṃ]  
     ye yena pahātabbā dhammā tesaṃ pahānañ cā ti imesu pana  
catusu ñāṇesu ye dhammā yena ñāṇena pahātabbā, tesaṃ  
pahānañ ca jānitabbaṃ| etāni hi yatāyogaṃ saṃyojana-  
kilesa-micchatta-lokadhamma-macchariya-vipallāsa-gantha-  
agati-āsava-ogha-yoga-nīvaraṇa-parāmāsa-upādāna-anusaya-  
mala-akusalakammapatha-cittuppādasankhātānaṃ dhammā-  
naṃ pahānakarāni|  
     tattha saṃyojanānī ti khandhehi khandhānaṃ phalena  
kammassa dukkhena vā sattānaṃ saṃyojakattā rūparāgā-  
dayo dasa dhammā vuccanti| yāvaṃ hi te, tāva etesaṃ  
anuparamo ti| tatrā pi: rūparāgo, anurūparāgo, māno,  
uddhaccaṃ avijjā ti ime pañca uddhaṃ nibbattanakakkhan-  
dhādisaṃyojakattā uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma| sak-
tea:visuddhimagga:22.p682.paraphrase: At the moment of the arahat path he emerges from the remaining fetters and latent tendencies (from lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance; the latent conceit, latent lust for existence, latent ignorance), from the defilements that follow them and the aggregates, and outwardly from all signs: as quoted, "understanding in the turning away by emerging in both ways is knowledge in the path". In the development of the eight worldly attainments calm is stronger; in developing the contemplation of impermanence and so on, insight is stronger; in the moment of the noble path they occur yoked together, neither exceeding the other; so in the four knowledges of the paths there is a joining of both powers. The text quotes the Paṭisambhidā: for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by restlessness and from the aggregates, one-pointedness of mind, non-distraction, is concentration whose domain is cessation; for one emerging from the defilements accompanied by ignorance, insight in the sense of contemplation has cessation as domain; thus in the sense of emerging calm and insight are of one taste, yoked and not exceeding each other. Then, under "what is to be abandoned by which, and the abandoning", the text begins: in these four knowledges one should know what states are to be abandoned by each knowledge, states that come as fetters, defilements, wrongnesses, worldly conditions, avarice, perversions, ties, wrong courses, taints, floods, yokes, hindrances, adherences, clingings, latent tendencies, stains, unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome thoughts. Fetters are ten things that bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; of them five are higher fetters (lust for fine-material existence, for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) (continued on p. 683).

tea:visuddhimagga:22.p683.title: Visuddhimagga
tea:visuddhimagga:22.p683.original:
kāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso, kāmarāgo, paṭi-  
gho ti ime pañca adhonibbattakakhandhādisaṃ yojakattā  
adhobhāgiyasaṃyojanāni nāma|  
     kilesā ti sayaṃ sankiliṭṭhattā sampayuttadhammānañ ca  
sankilesikattā lobho, doso, moho, māno, diṭṭhi, vicikicchā,  
thīnaṃ, uddhaccaṃ, ahitikaṃ, anottappan ti ime dasa  
dhammā|  
     micchattā ti micchā pavattanato micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsan-  
kappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchā-ājīvo, micchā-  
vāyāmo, micchāsati, micchāsamādhī ti ime aṭṭha dhammā|  
micchāviratti-micchāñāṇehi vā saddhiṃ dasa|  
     lokadhammā ti lokappavattiyā sati anuparamadhammattā1  
lābho, alābho, yaso, ayaso,2 sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, nindā, pasaṃsā  
ti ime aṭṭha| idha pana kāraṇūpacārena3 lābhādi-vatthu-  
kassa anunayassa alābhādi-vatthukassa paṭighassa c'; etaṃ  
lokadhammagahaṇena gahaṇaṃ katan ti veditabbaṃ|  
     macchariyānī ti āvāsamacchariyaṃ, kulamacchariyaṃ,  
lābhamacchariyaṃ, dhammamacchariyaṃ, vaṇṇamacchari-  
yan ti imāsu āvāsādisu aññesam sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahaṇā-  
kārena pavattāni pañca macchariyāni|  
     vipallāsā ti anicca-dukkha-anatta-asubhesu yeva vatthusu  
niccaṃ sukhaṃ attā subhan ti evaṃ pavatto saññāvipallāso,  
cittavipallāso, diṭṭhivipallāso ti ime tayo|  
     ganthā ti nāma kāyassa ceva rūpakāyassa ca ganthanato  
abhijjhādayo cattāro| tathā hi te abhijjhā-kāyagantho,  
vyāpādo-kāyagantho, sīlabbataparāmāso-kāyagantho, idaṃ-  
saccābhiniveso-kāyagantho icc'; eva vuttā|  
     agatī ti chanda-dosa-moha-bhayehi akattabbakaraṇassa  
kattabbākaraṇassa ca adhivacanaṃ| taṃ hi ariyehi agan-  
tabbattā agatī ti vuccati|  
     āsavā ti ārammaṇavasena āgotrabhūto ābhavaggato ca  
savanā-asaṃvutehi vā dvārehi ghaṭachiddehi, udakaṃ viya  
savanato niccapaggharaṇ'; aṭṭhena, saṃsāradukkhassa vā  
savanato kāmarāgabhavarāgamicchādiṭṭhi-āvijjānam etaṃ  
adhivacanaṃ|
tea:visuddhimagga:22.p683.paraphrase: The five lower fetters are personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust and ill will (paṭigha), which bind to lower aggregates and the like. Defilements (kilesa), being themselves defiled and defiling their associated states, are ten: greed, hate, delusion, conceit, view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, shamelessness and fearlessness of wrongdoing. Wrongnesses (micchatta) are eight: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration, or ten with wrong release and wrong knowledge. Worldly conditions (lokadhamma) are eight: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain, blame and praise; here the text says liking for what is gained and resentment for what is not gained are taken under those. Avarice (macchariya) is fivefold: over dwelling, family, gain, teaching and praise. Perversions (vipallāsa) are three: of perception, of mind and of view, taking the impermanent, painful, not-self and unlovely as permanent, pleasant, self and beautiful. Ties (gantha) are four: covetousness, ill will, adherence to rites and observances, and the insistence that "this alone is truth". Wrong courses (agati) are doing what should not be done and not doing what should be done through desire, hate, delusion and fear. Taints (āsava) is a name for sensual lust, lust for existence, wrong view and ignorance, so called because they flow out (as far as change-of-lineage and the top of existence by way of object, or through the unguarded doors like water through the holes of a jar, in the sense of constant trickling), or because they make the suffering of the round flow (continued on p. 684).

tea:yoga-bhasya:2.22.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.22.original:
kṛtārtham ekaṃ puruṣaṃ prati dṛśyaṃ naṣṭam api nāśaṃ prāptam apy anaṣṭaṃ tadanyapuruṣasādhāraṇatvāt /
kuśalaṃ puruṣaṃ prati nāśaṃ prāptam apy akuśalān puruṣān prati na kṛtārtham iti teṣāṃ dṛśeḥ karmaviṣayatām āpannaṃ labhata eva pararūpeṇātmarūpam iti /
ataś ca dṛgdarśanaśaktyor nityatvād anādiḥ saṃyogo vyākhyāta iti /
tathā coktam --- dharmiṇām anādisaṃyogād dharmamātrāṇām apy anādiḥ saṃyoga iti. 2.22
saṃyogasvarūpābhidhitsayedaṃ sūtraṃ pravavṛte ---
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.22.paraphrase: For the one puruṣa whose purpose is done, the seen, though ceased, has not ceased, since it is common to other puruṣas. For the skilful puruṣa it has come to ceasing; but for the unskilful ones, whose purpose is not done, it obtains its own form through another's form, having become the object of their seeing. So, since the two powers, of seeing and of sight, are eternal, the conjunction has been explained as beginningless. And it is said: 'From the beginningless conjunction of the property-bearers, the conjunction of the mere properties too is beginningless.'

tea:yoga-bhasya:2.5.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.5.original:
anitye kārye nityakhyātiḥ /
tadyathā --- dhruvā pṛthivī, dhruvā sacandratārakā dyauḥ, amṛtā divaukasa iti /
tathāśucau paramabībhatse kāye, ---
"sthānād bījād upaṣṭambhān niḥsyandān nidhanād api /
kāyam ādheyaśaucatvāt paṇḍitā hy aśuciṃ viduḥ" //
iti aśucau śucikhyātir dṛśyate /
naveva śaśāṅkalekhā kamanīyeyaṃ kanyā madhvamṛtāvayavanirmiteva candraṃ bhittvā niḥsṛteva jñāyate, nīlotpalapatrāyatākṣī hāvagarbhābhyāṃ locanābhyāṃ jīvalokam āśvāsayantīveti kasya kenābhisaṃbandhaḥ /
bhavati caivam aśucau śuciviparyāsapratyaya iti /
etenāpuṇye puṇyapratyayas tathaivānarthe cārthapratyayo vyākhyātaḥ /
tathā duḥkhe sukhakhyātiṃ vakṣyati --- "pariṇāmatāpasaṃskāraduḥkhair guṇavṛttivirodhāc ca duḥkham eva sarvaṃ vivekinaḥ" iti /
tatra sukhakhyātir avidyā /
tathānātmany ātmakhyātir bāhyopakaraṇeṣu cetanācetaneṣu bhogādhiṣṭhāne vā śarīre puruṣopakaraṇe vā manasy anātmany ātmakhyātir iti /
tathaitad atroktam --- "vyaktam avyaktaṃ vā sattvam ātmatvenābhipratītya tasya saṃpadam anu nandaty ātmasaṃpadaṃ manvānas tasya vyāpadam anu śocaty ātmavyāpadaṃ manvānaḥ sa sarvo 'pratibuddhaḥ" iti /
eṣā catuṣpadā bhavaty avidyā mūlam asya kleśasaṃtānasya karmāśayasya ca savipākasyeti /
tasyāś cāmitrāgoṣpadavadvastusatattvaṃ vijñeyam /
yathā nāmitro mitrābhāvo na mitramātraṃ kiṃtu tadviruddhaḥ sapatnaḥ /
yathā vāgoṣpadaṃ na goṣpadābhāvo na goṣpadamātraṃ kiṃtu deśa eva tābhyām anyad vastvantaram /
evam avidyā na pramāṇaṃ na pramāṇābhāvaḥ kiṃtu vidyāviparītaṃ jñānāntaram avidyeti
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.5.paraphrase: Ignorance is the appearing of permanence in an impermanent effect: e.g. 'the earth is fixed; the sky with moon and stars is fixed; the dwellers in heaven are immortal.' Likewise the appearing of purity in the impure, the utterly disgusting body — 'the wise know the body to be impure because of its place, its seed, its support, its outflow, its end, and because its purity has to be supplied' [quoted verse]. The text illustrates this with a young woman who is perceived (jñāyate) as lovely, 'like a new crescent of the moon, as if made of honey and nectar', and asks what is connected with what (kasya kena abhisaṃbandhaḥ); so arises the inverted cognition (viparyāsa-pratyaya) of the pure in the impure. By this the cognition of merit in demerit and of the useful in the useless is also explained. Likewise the appearing of pleasure in pain; the sūtra will say later [YS 2.15]: 'everything is suffering for the discerning, because of the sufferings of transformation, torment and impression, and because of the conflict of the functions of the guṇas'. And the appearing of self in the not-self: in external instruments, sentient or insentient (cetana-acetana), in the body as the seat of enjoyment, in the puruṣa's instrument, the mind (manas). It is said here: 'One who takes sattva, manifest or unmanifest, to be self rejoices at its prosperity, thinking it his own prosperity, and grieves at its calamity, thinking it his own calamity; he is wholly unawakened (apratibuddha).' This fourfold ignorance is the root of the whole chain of afflictions and of the store of karma with its ripening. Its true nature is to be understood like 'non-friend' (amitra) and 'cow-track' (goṣpada): as a non-friend is neither the absence of a friend nor merely a friend but a rival opposed to him, and a cow-track is neither the absence of a cow's track nor the mere track but a place different from both, so ignorance is neither valid cognition nor the absence of valid cognition, but another cognition contrary to knowledge (vidyā).

tea:yoga-bhasya:2.6.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.6.original:
puruṣo dṛkśaktir buddhir darśanaśaktir ity etayor ekasvarūpāpattir ivāsmitā kleśa ucyate /
bhoktṛbhogyaśaktyor atyantavibhaktayor atyantāsaṃkīrṇayor avibhāgaprāptāv iva satyāṃ bhogaḥ kalpate /
svarūpapratilambhe tu tayoḥ kaivalyam eva bhavati kuto bhoga iti /
tathā coktam --- "buddhitaḥ paraṃ puruṣam ākāraśīlavidyādibhir vibhaktam apaśyan kuryāt tatrātmabuddhiṃ mohena" iti
tea:yoga-bhasya:2.6.paraphrase: The puruṣa is the power of the seer (dṛk-śakti); the buddhi is the power of seeing (darśana-śakti). The seeming coming-together of the two into a single form is called the affliction I-am-ness. When the powers of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, utterly distinct and utterly unmixed, are as if reached in non-separation, then enjoyment (bhoga) is possible. But when they attain their own forms, only kaivalya comes about; where would enjoyment be? It is also said: 'One who does not see the puruṣa beyond the buddhi as distinct by form, conduct, knowledge and the like will make a self-notion (ātma-buddhi) there through delusion (moha).'

tea:yoga-sutra:2.20.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:2.20.paraphrase: The seer is seeing alone (dṛśi-mātra); though pure, it looks on cognitions (pratyaya).

tea:yoga-sutra:2.22.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:2.22.original: kṛtārthaṃ prati naṣṭam apy anaṣṭaṃ tadanyasādhāraṇatvāt
tea:yoga-sutra:2.22.paraphrase: Though it has ceased for one whose purpose is accomplished (kṛtārtha), it has not ceased, since it is common to others.

tea:yoga-sutra:2.25.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:2.25.paraphrase: From the absence of that (ignorance), the conjunction is absent; this is the abandonment (hāna), the seer's isolation (kaivalya).

tea:yoga-sutra:2.5.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:2.5.paraphrase: Ignorance (avidyā) is taking the impermanent (anitya), the impure (aśuci), the painful (duḥkha) and the not-self (anātman) to be permanent (nitya), pure (śuci), pleasant (sukha) and self (ātman).

tea:yoga-sutra:2.6.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:2.6.paraphrase: I-am-ness (asmitā) is the seeming identity of the power of the seer (dṛk-śakti) and the power of seeing (darśana-śakti).

tea:yoga-sutra:4.18.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
tea:yoga-sutra:4.18.paraphrase: The modifications of the mind are always known, because their lord, puruṣa, is unchanging.

summary: You described a pattern that the texts name: Māna (conceit), in the Buddhist texts. Each is shown below with your own words and the texts' description.

points.text: Read through the Vedic and yogic texts, your words “What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team” come closest to what they call Āsurī sampad (the demonic endowment) (a partial match for Māna (conceit)). Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born to the demonic endowment (BhG 16.4); it leads to bondage (16.5).

Your words “What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team” fit only loosely what the Buddhist texts call Māna (conceit). Vism XXII: the fetters are ten states, beginning with lust for form, so called because they bind aggregates to aggregates, action to its fruit, and beings to suffering. Lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness and ignorance are the five higher fetters; personality view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual lust and resentment are the five lower fetters.

Each names a false or inflated 'I'. YS: I-am-ness is the seeming identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing (YS 2.6). Vyāsa: the puruṣa is the seer's power, the buddhi the power of seeing (YB 2.6). Gītā: arrogance and conceit (darpa, abhimāna) belong to the demonic endowment (BhG 16.4), which leads to bondage (BhG 16.5). TS: pride (māna) is one of the four passions (TS 8.9), by which the soul takes in karmic matter (TS 8.2). Visuddhimagga: personality view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) regards form and the other aggregates as self (Vism XVII) and is one of the five lower fetters; conceit (māna) is a defilement and a fetter that remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). Under the one-truth principle, they describe it from different standpoints: the match is a partial match, not an identity.

differences.text: On the sense of 'I': Jain, Yoga, Upaniṣadic and Buddhist texts all teach that one is not the body, nor any passing state of mind. The Yoga Sūtra calls the seer's seeming oneness with the mind 'I-am-ness'; Theravāda texts teach seeing 'this is not mine, I am not this'. They differ on what is left: Jain texts, many souls whose changing states are their own; the Yoga Sūtra, many seers that never change; the Upaniṣads, a self that is brahman; Theravāda texts, nothing that is a self. These are different answers, not one.

Asmitā is not pride. YS 2.6 names a confusion of the seer with its instrument, a structural error that is present even without any haughtiness. The Gītā's darpa and abhimāna and the Jain māna are attitudes of self-exaltation: the Gītā lists them among the marks of a bad endowment (BhG 16.4), and TS grades māna in four intensities (TS 8.9). They meet only in the 'I'. Personality view comes closest to asmitā, since both take something that is not the self as the self. The Yoga also counts that as an error (YS 2.5), but it corrects the error by isolating a real seer (YS 2.25). The Visuddhimagga's remedy is to abandon the view, which is one of the five lower fetters, and conceit remains until the arahat path (Vism XXII). It does not isolate a seer in the view's place. Whether a seer remains is not yet reconciled (row ot:provisional-self-question of one_truth.json).

practices.name: Observing the sense fields and their fetter (MN 10:40)
practices.why: You wrote “What I actually want to look at is how I am with my team”. The texts pair what they call Māna (conceit) with this practice.
steps: Understand the eye, sights, and the fetter that arises dependent on both (MN 10:40).
Understand how a fetter not yet arisen comes to arise, how an arisen one is given up, and how once given up it does not arise again (MN 10:40).
Go through the ear and sounds, nose and smells, tongue and tastes, body and touches, mind and ideas in the same way (MN 10:40).

duration.basis: product default for a beginner; the text gives no length

warnings.text: The sutta's condition for every contemplation: one meditates 'keen, aware and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world'.
Nearest general caution in the same discourse family: 'There is no development of mindfulness of breathing for someone who is unmindful and lacks awareness' (said of breathing mindfulness).
